- Investigate U009.

I have enough evidence. Let me think about U009: post-hoc temporal re-ranking vs. version-level contamination measurement. Evidence gathered:
- Legal retrieval literature prescribes bitemporal correctness (concept), no empirical comparison (arxiv:2606.09724 explicitly).
- LEGAL-LINK-EU benchmark encodes temporal validity but MCQA, not retrieval (arxiv:2608.21409).
- Ontology-governed legal RAG filters by temporal validity (doi:10.3390/computers15080471) — abstract only.
- Temporal retrieval systems: fixed three-signal hybrid (ssrn.7174868), Chronofy learned decay (iri), TempFinRAG hard as-of (sym18091498).
- Regulatory static retrieval benchmark (ssrn.7087840); legal retrieval benchmark static (Nor-CaseHOLD ssrn.6459080).
- Survey: legal QA static; temporal retrieval open (arxiv:2505.20243).

Gaps (evidence-linked):
G1: No version-level retrieval evaluation over amended legal text with near-duplicate successive revisions, validity intervals, and time-stamped queries; existing legal benchmarks are static or MCQA (evidence: survey p.24 quote, 2606.09724 no empirical comparison + bitemporal requirements, 2608.21409 MCQA encoding temporal validity, 7087840 static questions, 6459080 static benchmark). Why unaddressed: temporal legal work is conceptual/prescriptive or MCQA; regulatory retrieval benchmarks have no target dates; temporal benchmarks are ESG/finance. Research question: does explicit valid-time-aware re-ranking reduce version confusion (superseded/not-yet-in-force retrieval) relative to semantic-only retrieval on near-duplicate amended clauses? Potential experiment: build the benchmark, evaluate.

G2: No empirical test of whether temporal re-ranking transfers across base retrievers, and no measurement of whether the temporal signal should be graded decay or hard as-of validity. Evidence: closest systems hard-code; RMA shows hybrid not uniformly best; Chronofy/Bridging use decay, TempFinRAG uses hard boundary; survey flags recency bias. Why unaddressed: each system implements one signal in one pipeline; no head-to-head.

G3 (maybe): Answer accuracy is insensitive to version confusion; need contamination metric for legal text — evidence TempFinRAG temporal leakage metric exists in finance but not applied to legal versioned retrieval. This is kind of part of G1.

I'll record 2 gaps (G1, G2) — maybe 3. Evidence requires quotes where possible; I have verified quotes from claims C002, C004, C012, C013, C014, C016, C018 and RMA (need quote? I can cite abstract without quote, support indirect).

Let me record G1 and G2 (and maybe G3 = measurement). Keep to 2-3.

Modifications (2-5), with recommended=true for the strongest:
M1: Replace recency decay with validity-interval (as-of) temporal relevance: rank by valid-time membership ("in force at target date") combined with graded semantic score; include hard as-of filter as candidate set definition and graded tie-break. Why differs from closest: Bridging/Chronofy use elapsed-time decay; TempFinRAG uses hard boundary inside a multimodal pipeline. Mechanism: temporal term = 1 if target_date ∈ [effective_from, effective_to) else penalize; within valid set, semantic score primary or a small recency bonus. Expected benefit: avoids demoting long-lived in-force clauses; addresses the documented confounder. Novelty: hedged — the valid-time notion is pre-empted conceptually (bitemporal correctness), so novelty is in the empirical demonstration and cross-retriever transfer, not the concept. Implementation difficulty moderate (needs validity intervals); experimental difficulty moderate. Main risk: validity metadata granularity.
M2: Cross-retriever transfer study + interaction analysis: apply the same temporal re-ranking to BM25, dense, hybrid; ablate temporal signal forms (none / decay / as-of / as-of+decay); report per-retriever gains. Why differs: no existing work does cross-retriever transfer. Novelty hedged: framing anticipated by "architecture-agnostic" but no empirical transfer study. Difficulty: low implementation, moderate experimental (need multiple retrievers, but standard tools).
M3: Version-level contamination metric as primary: define and report temporal contamination (superseded/not-yet-in-force passages retrieved/used) and near-duplicate version confusion, in addition to answer accuracy; construct query set that decouples recency from correctness (include historical/mid-chain target dates) plus a recency-only baseline. Why differs: legal benchmarks are static/MCQA; temporal leakage metric exists in finance only. Difficulty: low-moderate. Recommended? This is the core of the residual gap.
M4: Bitemporal (valid time vs transaction time) legal retrieval evaluation: incorporate both effective dates and enactment/record dates, following ELI; test whether using transaction time (version publication) vs valid time changes results. Why differs: existing decay systems conflate time with age; the legal framework paper prescribes bitemporal but gives no empirical comparison. Difficulty: high implementation (needs both timestamps), high experimental. Novelty modest-high.
M5 maybe: Hybrid validity-gated candidate set + learned combination? Might overlap M1. Keep 4 modifications.

Recommended: I think M1 combined with M3 is strongest. But must pick one recommended=true. The strongest single direction: "Validity-gated temporal re-ranking with version-level contamination evaluation" — maybe merge M1 and M3? The instruction: one modification recommended. Let me make M3 the recommended one? Hmm. The residual defensible delta is the measurement + cross-retriever demonstration. M1 (validity instead of recency) is a method change that directly addresses the biggest technical risk. I'd recommend M1 as the strongest: "replace elapsed-time decay with validity-interval as-of relevance (valid-time gating)" — because it fixes the wrong inductive bias and is the mechanism that makes the hypothesis plausible. But its novelty is lower (concept pre-empted). M2 (cross-retriever transfer) is the least-occupied novelty. Hmm.

Which is strongest for making the idea distinct AND valid? I'd say a combined framing: M1 as the mechanism (validity-gated) plus M2 as the study design (cross-retriever). But record_modification is per-modification; I can make one modification that combines: "Validity-gated temporal re-ranking evaluated across retrievers" — but then it's a mix. Better: recommend M2? Let me think about what the next step should be: an experiment plan. The modification that most strengthens: M2 (cross-retriever transfer + signal ablation) is the unoccupied novelty; M1 alone might be seen as applying known bitemporal concept. But M1 is required for correctness.

I'll set recommended=true for M2 ("Retrieval-agnostic temporal signal, evaluated across base retrievers with a signal-form ablation"), because it directly instantiates the idea's one surviving distinction (retrieval-agnostic), and it inherently includes comparing decay vs as-of (M1's signal) as an ablation. Hmm, but then M1's mechanism change is folded in as an ablation arm. That's elegant: M2 = cross-retriever × temporal-signal-form factorial. Let me define M2 that way and recommend it. Actually let me restructure:

M1: Validity-interval (valid-time) temporal relevance instead of elapsed-time decay. (mechanism fix)
M2: Cross-retriever × temporal-signal factorial evaluation (recommended). (surviving novelty: retrieval-agnostic demonstration; includes decay vs as-of vs hybrid as arms)
M3: Version-level contamination metric + recency-decoupled query design (measurement fix)
M4: Bitemporal (valid vs transaction time) evaluation with ELI dates (extension)

Recommended = M2. Good.

input.gap: No retrieval benchmark evaluates version selection over continuously amended legal text at clause granularity: no resource pairs time-stamped queries with ground-truth in-force versions of overlapping, near-duplicate amended clauses and measures retrieval of superseded or not-yet-in-force text. Legal-domain temporal work is either conceptual/prescriptive (explicitly without empirical comparison) or multiple-choice over normative-act relationships without source-text retrieval; temporal retrieval benchmarks with temporal-accuracy metrics exist only for ESG disclosures and financial filings; regulatory retrieval benchmarks have no target dates at all.
input.potential_experiment: Construct a version-level benchmark from a jurisdiction with machine-readable amendment metadata (e.g., EU legislation under ELI, which encodes date of entry into force and date of applicability): retrieve clauses from a versioned corpus where successive versions are near-duplicates; annotate queries with a target date and the ground-truth in-force clause version, deliberately including target dates whose authoritative version is not the latest; evaluate semantic-only, recency-decay, hard as-of filtering, and valid-time gated re-ranking, reporting version-level temporal contamination alongside answer accuracy.
input.research_question: On a corpus of continuously amended statutes/regulations with near-duplicate successive versions, does valid-time-aware (as-of) temporal re-ranking reduce retrieval of superseded or not-yet-in-force clauses, and improve answer accuracy, compared with semantic-only retrieval and with a recency-decay baseline?
input.verification_required: Re-run literature searches (the paper budget for this session is exhausted) for any amended-statute retrieval benchmark, and confirm that passage/clause-level validity metadata (not only legislation-level dates) can be extracted for the chosen jurisdiction and corpus snapshot.
input.why_unaddressed: The temporal QA survey states legal QA datasets are static and do not address the temporal dynamics of legal knowledge; the legal-retrieval framework that formalizes the requirement ('diachronic blindness', 'bitemporal correctness') states explicitly that it reports no benchmarked empirical comparison and is formal and diagnostic; the legal benchmark that encodes temporal validity is a multiple-choice diagnostic that does not evaluate retrieval of source text; the point-in-time evaluation protocol with a temporal-leakage metric exists only for financial filings; and the regulatory retrieval benchmark has no target-date or version dimension.

evidence.quote: We propose a three-signal hybrid framework integrating BM25 lexical matching, dense semantic embeddings, and exponential temporal decay, which achieves 99.8% temporal accuracy and 50.8% entity precision across all three languages
Layer 2 integrates learnable exponential decay functions into graph-based retrieval
BM25 outperforms hybrid on multihop queries (ROUGE-L 0.304 vs. 0.239)

input.gap: No controlled comparison varies both the base retriever and the form of the temporal signal: each published temporal-retrieval system hard-codes one temporal mechanism inside one pipeline (exponential decay inside a fixed three-signal hybrid; learnable decay inside graph-based retrieval; a hard as-of boundary inside a multimodal verifier), and the temporal pathologies are asserted to be architecture-agnostic without a transfer measurement. It is therefore unknown whether temporal re-ranking gains persist across BM25, dense and hybrid retrievers, and whether graded recency decay or valid-time membership is the appropriate signal for amended normative text.
input.potential_experiment: A factorial evaluation on a single held-out query set: base retriever in {BM25, dense, hybrid RRF} x temporal signal in {none, recency decay, valid-time gating, valid-time gating + semantic re-rank}, with matched retrieval depth and reader, reporting temporal contamination, nDCG/recall and answer accuracy per cell, plus a recency-only baseline and a hard as-of baseline.
input.research_question: How do the gains from temporal re-ranking over amended normative text vary across base retrievers (BM25, dense, hybrid) and temporal signal forms (none, recency decay, valid-time membership), and does any form dominate consistently?
input.verification_required: Confirm by citation/full-text inspection that none of the closest systems reports a cross-retriever transfer study (the two closest were abstract-only here), and re-check recent literature once the search budget allows.
input.why_unaddressed: The three closest systems each integrate temporal handling into one architecture, and the legal framework paper that calls the pathologies architecture-agnostic reports no empirical comparison. The only retrieved regulatory comparison of sparse/dense/hybrid shows hybrid is not uniformly best (BM25 wins on multihop), which indicates base-retriever choice matters but was not tested with a temporal component.

input.description: Replace the elapsed-time (recency-decay) temporal term with valid-time membership: a passage's temporal relevance is determined by whether the query's target date falls inside the clause's in-force interval [effective_from, effective_to), with hard exclusion of not-yet-in-force and superseded clauses before semantic ranking. Recency decay is retained only as an explicit comparison arm rather than the default signal.
input.expected_benefit: Removes the failure mode in which a recent but superseded or not-yet-in-force amendment outranks a long-lived in-force clause; makes the hypothesis plausible for point-in-time legal questions rather than only for news-like recency questions.
input.experimental_difficulty_basis: Requires per-clause in-force intervals and a query set whose authoritative version is deliberately not always the latest; evaluation itself reuses standard retrievers and a fixed reader.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: Validity intervals must be parsed or reconstructed from amendment metadata; the retrieval-side change is a simple candidate filter plus score adjustment and needs no retraining.
input.main_risk: Passage-level validity metadata may be unavailable or noisy, and if only legislation-level dates exist the valid-time gate degenerates into a coarse document filter that neither helps nor hurts.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: the valid-time/bitemporal requirement is already stated conceptually in the legal-retrieval literature, so novelty would rest on the empirical demonstration that valid-time gating outperforms recency decay for near-duplicate amended clauses, not on the concept.
required_baselines: Semantic-only retrieval with the same base retriever
input.title: Validity-gated (valid-time) temporal relevance instead of elapsed-time decay
input.why_differs: The closest systems use exponential decay or learnable decay as the temporal signal, which equates age with loss of validity; TempFinRAG uses a hard as-of boundary but inside a multimodal financial pipeline. This modification makes valid-time membership the temporal term itself, in a retriever-independent layer, and treats decay as merely one ablation arm.

input.hypothesis: For time-specific queries over continuously amended regulatory text, an explicitly valid-time-aware, retrieval-agnostic re-ranking layer reduces retrieval of superseded or not-yet-in-force near-duplicate clauses and improves answer accuracy relative to the same base retriever with semantic similarity alone, and outperforms elapsed-time decay; the size of the gain depends on the base retriever and on how often the authoritative version is not the most recent.
input.rationale: The evidence shows the original framing is largely pre-empted: semantic-plus-exponential-decay hybrid retrieval with a temporal benchmark is published, learnable decay in retrieval is published, the valid-time/bitemporal requirement is already articulated in legal-retrieval theory, a legal benchmark encoding temporal validity exists, and a legal RAG system already filters sources by temporal validity. What is not covered anywhere found is (1) an empirical cross-retriever transfer study of a temporal layer, (2) version-level contamination measurement on near-duplicate amended legal clauses, and (3) a measured comparison of recency decay against valid-time membership on such a corpus, with queries decoupled from recency. The original mechanism (elapsed-time decay) is also the weakest part on independent grounds, since a superseded clause can be the temporally nearest one. Narrowing scope this way keeps a testable, non-pre-empted contribution while fixing the mechanism; it deserves investigation next because it can be falsified cheaply and would still produce a useful negative result about when temporal re-ranking helps.

Let me re-issue the 4 modifications with technical_mechanism.

M1 technical_mechanism: "Compute per-clause in-force interval [effective_from, effective_to) from amendment metadata; define temporal relevance tau(q,p)=1 if target_date in interval else 0; final score = semantic_score * tau (or semantic score with excluded passages removed), optionally adding a small graded bonus for clauses whose validity window most tightly contains the target date. No retraining; applied after the base retriever returns candidates."

M2 technical_mechanism: "Wrap each base retriever (BM25, dense encoder, hybrid RRF) behind a common interface; for each cell, re-rank the same candidate pool with the selected temporal term and pass the top-k to a fixed reader; compute contamination, ranking and answer metrics per cell; use identical retrieval depth, chunking, embedding model and prompt across cells."

M3 technical_mechanism: "Tag every corpus passage with a status relative to the query target date (in-force / superseded / not-yet-in-force) from its validity interval; contamination = fraction of retrieved (or cited) passages not in force at the target date; version-confusion = retrieved passage is a different version of the gold clause. Query sampling stratifies on whether the gold version is the latest, with a dedicated non-latest subset."

M4 technical_mechanism: "Store two dates per clause: valid-time start/end (entry into force, applicability) and transaction-time date (record publication); define separate temporal terms from each; evaluate ranking under valid-time membership, transaction-time ordering, and decay from each axis; restrict the informative subset to clauses where the axes diverge (retroactive or delayed-application provisions)."

input.experimental_difficulty_basis: Requires per-clause in-force intervals and a query set whose authoritative version is deliberately not always the latest; evaluation itself reuses standard retrievers and a fixed reader.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: Validity intervals must be parsed or reconstructed from amendment metadata; the retrieval-side change is a simple candidate filter plus score adjustment and needs no retraining.
input.main_risk: Passage-level validity metadata may be unavailable or noisy, and if only legislation-level dates exist the valid-time gate degenerates into a coarse document filter that neither helps nor hurts.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: the valid-time/bitemporal requirement is already stated conceptually in the legal-retrieval literature, so novelty would rest on the empirical demonstration that valid-time gating outperforms recency decay for near-duplicate amended clauses, not on the concept.
required_baselines: Semantic-only retrieval with the same base retriever
input.technical_mechanism: Derive a per-clause in-force interval [effective_from, effective_to) from amendment metadata (e.g., entry-into-force and applicability dates under a legal identifier standard). Define a temporal gate tau(q,p)=1 if target_date(q) is in the interval, else 0. Apply the gate to the base retriever's candidate list before scoring (or multiply it into the final score) so only in-force clauses are ranked, then rank by the base retriever's semantic/lexical score; optionally add a small graded tie-break favouring the clause whose validity window most tightly contains the target date. No retraining and no change to the base retriever; the layer sits between candidate generation and top-k selection.
input.title: Validity-gated (valid-time) temporal relevance instead of elapsed-time decay
input.why_differs: The closest systems use exponential decay or learnable decay as the temporal signal, which equates age with loss of validity; TempFinRAG uses a hard as-of boundary but inside a multimodal financial pipeline. This modification makes valid-time membership the temporal term itself, in a retriever-independent layer, and treats decay as merely one ablation arm.

input.description: Evaluate the temporal re-ranking layer as a factor over base retrievers and signal forms on one held-out query set: base retriever in {BM25, dense, hybrid RRF} x temporal signal in {none, recency decay, valid-time gating, valid-time gating plus tie-break}, with matched retrieval depth, embedding model and reader, reporting per-cell temporal contamination, nDCG/recall and answer accuracy.
input.expected_benefit: Turns the retrieval-agnostic claim from framing into measurement, tests whether base-retriever choice interacts with the temporal signal, and supplies the cross-retriever evidence no reviewed system provides.
input.experimental_difficulty_basis: A full factorial needs a fixed corpus, query set and reader plus careful budget matching across cells; all components are standard and cheap, but the design must avoid confounding retriever strength with temporal signal.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: Base retrievers (BM25, dense encoder, RRF hybrid) and evaluation harness patterns are public and reusable; only the temporal layer is new code.
input.main_risk: Results may be uninteresting if temporal re-ranking helps uniformly or not at all; and gains may be dominated by retriever choice rather than the temporal term, which would reduce the contribution to a negative/scope result.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: no retrieved work performs a cross-retriever transfer study of temporal re-ranking, so the empirical result would be new even though the phrase 'architecture-agnostic' already appears in the legal-retrieval literature.
required_baselines: Each base retriever without any temporal term (semantic-only / lexical-only)
Published three-signal hybrid as an external reference point
input.technical_mechanism: Put BM25, a dense encoder and an RRF hybrid behind one retrieval interface returning a ranked candidate pool at a fixed depth. For each cell, apply the selected temporal term to the same candidate pool and pass the top-k to a fixed reader LLM with a fixed prompt. Hold chunking, embedding model, retrieval depth and reader constant across cells so the temporal signal and base retriever are the only manipulated factors; compute version-level contamination, ranking metrics and answer accuracy per cell, with paired significance tests across the shared query set.
input.title: Cross-retriever, signal-form factorial evaluation of the temporal layer
input.why_differs: Every reviewed temporal system integrates its temporal mechanism into a single pipeline, so the transfer claim is unmeasured; this design makes the base retriever and the temporal signal independent factors. It also directly tests the recency-versus-validity contradiction, which is currently split across papers rather than compared.

input.description: Make version-level temporal contamination a primary outcome: for each query and each retrieved passage, label whether it is in force, superseded, or not yet in force at the target date, and report contamination rate and near-duplicate version-confusion alongside answer accuracy. Construct the query set so that a substantial share of queries have an authoritative version that is not the most recent, and always report a pure recency-only baseline.
input.expected_benefit: Removes the confound that answer accuracy is blind when the superseded version yields the same answer text; prevents a trivial recency prior from masquerading as temporal relevance; makes the mechanism claim falsifiable.
input.experimental_difficulty_basis: Requires careful annotation of the in-force version per query (or reliable automated derivation), plus a deliberate sampling strategy for non-latest authoritative versions; the metric computation itself is straightforward.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: The metric is a rule over retrieved passage ids and their validity intervals; the adaptation is conceptually straightforward from point-in-time financial QA's temporal-leakage metric.
input.main_risk: If near-duplicate versions genuinely produce identical answers, even the contamination metric may show small differences on end-task quality; the honest result may be a measurement paper rather than an accuracy-improvement paper.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: temporal-leakage-style metrics exist in point-in-time financial QA, but no retrieved work applies version-contamination measurement to amended legal text, and no reviewed benchmark decouples recency from correctness.
required_baselines: Recency-only ranking (always prefer the latest version)
input.technical_mechanism: Tag every corpus passage with a status relative to the target date derived from its validity interval: in-force, superseded, or not-yet-in-force. Define contamination as the fraction of retrieved (and of reader-cited) passages that are not in force at the target date, and version confusion as retrieving a different version of the gold clause. Sample queries in strata defined by whether the gold in-force version is the latest, including a dedicated non-latest stratum whose target dates lie before later amendments; compare all systems on the same stratified query set with a recency-only ranker as an explicit control.
input.title: Version-confusion metric with recency-decoupled queries and a recency-only baseline
input.why_differs: Legal benchmarks found in the review are static or multiple-choice and do not evaluate which version of a clause is retrieved; the closest temporal metrics measure answer accuracy or (in finance) evidence leakage. This modification makes the version-selection error the measured quantity and forces the design to separate recency from validity.

input.description: Model both legal time axes explicitly: valid time (when a clause produces legal effect) and transaction time (when the version entered the official record), following the legal informatics standard that encodes date of entry into force and date of applicability. Compare ranking by valid time, by transaction time, and by elapsed time from each, to test whether the two axes are interchangeable for retrieval.
input.expected_benefit: Directly tests the bitemporal requirement that legal-retrieval theory prescribes but no retrieved work evaluates empirically, and identifies which timestamp a practical system must index.
input.experimental_difficulty_basis: Requires two timestamp fields per clause, a corpus where they diverge (retroactive or delayed-application provisions), and a query set sensitive to the distinction; such cases may be rare and hard to annotate.
input.implementation_difficulty_basis: Both date fields are standard in legal identifiers for some jurisdictions, but normalizing them across a corpus and aligning them with clause granularity is non-trivial.
input.main_risk: If valid time and transaction time coincide for most clauses in the chosen corpus, the comparison is uninformative and the modification yields no measurable difference.
input.potential_novelty: Hedged: the bitemporal distinction is already articulated conceptually in legal-retrieval theory, so the contribution would be the first empirical comparison of the two axes for retrieval, not the distinction itself.
required_baselines: Valid-time membership (as in the validity-gated arm)
input.technical_mechanism: Store two timestamps per clause: valid-time bounds (entry into force, applicability start/end) and a transaction-time date (official record publication). Define independent temporal terms from each axis and evaluate four rankers over the same candidate pool: valid-time membership, transaction-time ordering, decay from valid time, and decay from transaction time. Restrict the informative analysis to clauses where the axes diverge (retroactive or delayed-application provisions) so the comparison has power, and report results separately for that subset.
input.title: Bitemporal evaluation: valid time versus transaction time as the ranking signal
input.why_differs: Existing decay-based systems conflate a single document timestamp with age; the legal-retrieval framework that prescribes bitemporal correctness offers no empirical comparison. This modification makes the two axes an experimental factor rather than an architectural assumption.
